Writing a Game Boy emulator from nothing, with the picture unit modelled dot by dot, is hard. Ours passes all 24 mealybug tests: pictures that must match photographs of the real hardware, pixel for pixel. It passes Mooneye, 97 of 97, and Blargg, 51 of 51, and ranks #1 on the public Game Boy accuracy board, level with DocBoy. On the two newer Color suites, cgb-acid-hell and the AGE tests, it scores ahead of every other emulator we measured. It runs many licensed and unlicensed cartridge chips, the Super Game Boy, the Pocket Camera, and nearly every Game Boy and Color game we tested.

Then we ran the hardest test there is: deterministic synthesis from documentation alone. A builder who had never seen our code was given our pages and nothing else, and built a Game Boy emulator from them. Its output was identical to ours on 170 of 170 tests, every mealybug and AGE test among them. When documentation is precise enough that the machine can be rebuilt from the words alone, the documentation is the blueprint.

We then did the same on many more systems. Every result, dated, with the fingerprint of the exact file this site serves, is below under Checked by rebuilding.

The little game tiles scattered through your library are not screenshots or GIFs. They are the actual games, running live, with the demo loops attracting you in exactly like they did on a shop shelf in 1991. Walk past them in your movie collection and they are playing.

The proof

11 emulators, one home server

Every emulator here is fed by one small server that is yours, running on your own computer. Point it at your game library and that is the whole setup: no emulator cores to install, no paths, no launch commands, no scraper accounts. It recognises every cartridge by its fingerprint and picks the right start-up firmware for it. Box art, logos and manuals arrive on their own, with no scraping and no daily limits. Plug in a controller and it just works, with A where your controller says A. At home it serves the whole collection to every screen in the house, and your games keep playing even locally with no internet. Away from home, your vault code brings the same collection to you anywhere online.

Secure. Versatile. Simple.

From the silicon up

We build these ourselves. From nothing.

Most emulators are handed down. Someone reverse-engineers a machine once, and everyone else spends twenty years patching, porting, and inheriting every shortcut from that original code.

That is not what we do here.

We do not research these machines to build them. We build them to research them.

This is a preservation project first and foremost. Reconstructing a system from nothing is the ultimate form of hardware study because every chip must be fully understood before it can be rebuilt, with no prior work to fall back on. When you build from scratch, you truly understand the machine instead of trusting decades-old assumptions.

That philosophy produced the world's first emulator for the modern ARM Game & Watch, covering the Zelda and Mario twins running on the STM32H7. With no existing code to copy or core to fork, we reverse-engineered the hardware and built it from the silicon up, executing the real internal firmware directly in the browser.

We are bringing that same standard to how retro media is experienced. Emulation today remains fragmented, tied to legacy builds, complex setups, and fragile workarounds. We are creating a single home for games and media together that simply works on any modern device with zero setup. Achieving that seamless experience requires hand-rolled, clean emulators rather than decades of stitched-together patches.

What we learn along the way does not stay buried in code. We write documentation precise enough that someone can build a working emulator from our words alone. We proved this approach by writing a complete Game Boy specification covering all 24 mealybug edge-case tests, then building an emulator solely from those words with no source code or external references. It compiled and passed every test on the first attempt. We have done the same for many more systems since, each one listed in the table below.

The emulator itself serves as the ultimate test of accuracy, where any flaw in our hardware understanding or documentation is immediately exposed by the software.

Preservation

Why it matters

Every one of these machines belongs to all of us. A Game & Watch went into pockets in Osaka and in Manchester in the same few years. A Game Boy ate a fortune in AA batteries under the covers in bedrooms on every continent. A prototype almost nobody ever saw still shaped the machine that came after it. These games, and the films and shows sitting beside them, are how most of the world actually spent its evenings for forty years. That is shared culture, not private nostalgia. And it is disappearing, into landfill, into dead hard drives, into knowledge that leaves with the people who held it.

Preserving it properly means more than making it run. It means writing down exactly how these machines think, so precisely that anyone can rebuild them perfectly, forever. Not a copy of a copy of someone's old code, but a true tested blueprint. That is the difference between hoping it survives and making sure it does.

Where support goes

Help build it

This is built by one person, and doing it properly is not cheap. If this brought back the feeling of being a kid in front of a game you loved, you can help keep it alive and growing. Here is exactly where support goes.

Hardware and teardowns.

Reverse-engineering rare and obsolete machines means physically owning them. Tracking down obscure Game & Watch variants, dev kits and cartridges, plus the bench equipment to probe them, is a real budget for real hardware. This is where accurate discovery starts.

Hosting and bandwidth.

We do not host anyone's games or media. Your games and your movies stay yours, on your own storage, self hosted. What we host is the platform itself, the emulators and the site, and delivering that fast and seamlessly to any device needs quick, reliable hosting with no ads and no bloat.

Time to build it right.

Writing rigorous documentation, passing punishing torture tests, and building clean from a single blueprint takes hundreds of hours of deep focus. Support buys that focus, and lets the library keep growing instead of stalling.

Testing everywhere.

Making sure every module runs at full speed across browsers, phones and operating systems means constant optimisation and testing across a lot of different hardware.

Everything here stays free to use. Always.

Hardware Lineage

Nearly fifty years of play, on a single thread.

Every console on this site, handheld and home, laid out in the order it really arrived, from the Atari VCS in 1977 onwards: the four Ataris, the Game & Watch series, the Famicom, the NES and the Disk System, the Game Boy, the Game Boy Color and the Pokémon mini. The families overlap and cut across one another, because that is how the hardware actually happened. Tap any entry to drop into its catalogue.

About

The machines, in our words

CrystalWorlds.Media is a love letter to the machines that taught the world to play. It began as a home for one family, the small, strange Game & Watch handhelds Nintendo built between 1980 and 1991, and it has grown into a shelf of handhelds and home consoles, your own films and shows. Every emulator here was written from scratch by us, standing proudly on the shoulders of the community, researchers, and pioneer engineers who painfully mapped these systems before us. It is all brought to life right inside your browser.

It began with the first Game & Watch, Ball, which slipped out of Japan on April 9th, 1980. It cost a few thousand yen, ran on watch batteries, and let you keep a juggler from dropping two stiff little balls. It sold a million copies. By the time the line ended in 1991, Nintendo had shipped fifty-nine different models across ten distinct hardware series, and posted somewhere north of forty-three million units sold worldwide.

"Lateral thinking with withered technology." That was Gunpei Yokoi's design philosophy: take old, cheap, well-understood parts; find a brand-new use for them.

The man behind the magic.

Gunpei Yokoi joined Nintendo in 1965 as a maintenance engineer. He went on to lead the R&D1 group responsible for the Game & Watch, the Game Boy, and Metroid. The story goes that he watched a bored salaryman on a Shinkansen passing time by tapping the buttons of a calculator, and wondered if you could put a tiny game in the same pocket-sized shell. The Game & Watch is what came out the other side.

Yokoi left Nintendo in 1996 and his fingerprints are still on every handheld Nintendo ships, and on most of the machines on this page.

One client. Every screen.

All of it is fed by one small server that sits on your own computer. Point it at your library, and that is the whole setup: it recognises every cartridge by its fingerprint, picks the right start-up firmware, and maps your controller the instant it is plugged in. At home, it serves your entire collection to every screen in the house. Away from home, your vault code brings that same collection to you anywhere.

Built from nothing.

Most emulators are handed down: someone reverse-engineers a machine once, and everyone else inherits every shortcut and quirk from that original code. That is not what we do here. We do not research these machines to build them. We build them to research them.

Every core on this site was written from the chip makers' own documentation and from direct measurement of real hardware, with nothing copied from an existing emulator. The documentation we write along the way is precise enough that a second core, built solely from our words with no source code, passed every test on the first attempt. Where a public test exists, we publish our score beside everyone else's, complete with the date it was measured; where none exists, we write our own test cartridges, run them on real hardware, and show the results.

Suggestions and submissions.

Suggestions and submissions are welcome from anyone, on the project's GitHub page: a bug report, a fix, a correction to a Hardware or Emulation page, a measurement from real hardware, a game that does not play right, or an idea. Every submission is read and considered.

Games and firmware are never accepted. A submission that contains a game, a BIOS, a boot program or any other console firmware, or a link to one, is always rejected, whatever else it contains. This site plays only the files you already own, and it never ships, hosts or shares them.

Settings
Version 2.1.0
No passwords. No accounts. Just a vault code.

This site doesn't use logins or sign-ups. Instead, this browser holds a single random vault code (a UUID). The vault itself keeps only that code and, if you add one, a recovery email. Your play time, saves and settings stay in this browser, not in the vault. Anyone who knows the code can change or delete the vault; nobody else can. Save it in a password manager. If you lose the code and saved no recovery email, it cannot be found again: there's no password reset, because there's no password. Sponsors can choose to sign in with GitHub to read the Stories; nothing else here needs it.

Choose how the site looks. Dark is the default: it's like viewing the units in a dim room. Light brightens everything, and gives the see-through Crystal Screen units their proper light look. OLED is Dark with a pure black page and a black ground around the game picture, for screens that show true black. Your choice is remembered on this device.

The highlight colour used across the site: the glow when you hover a tile, the drawer's section headers, the play-time readout, buttons and links. The default is the classic green.

The playable emulators need each device's firmware, its segment artwork and (for the Mario and Zelda colour units) their flash firmware, none of which ships with the site. Open a single .zip of your own dumps, segment SVGs and colour-unit flash here, and the site identifies everything by its content and brings the emulators to life. It's all kept on this device; nothing is uploaded.

This code is the only key to your vault. Save it in a password manager. Anyone with it can change or delete your vault.

Generates a brand-new vault code and replaces the current one. Your recovery email stays with the vault and this browser's play time carries over; only the code changes. Save the new code immediately: if you lose it, only a saved recovery email can get it back.

If this browser forgets your vault code or sign-ins, this shows what it still holds, which address you are on and whether the browser has agreed to keep the site's data. It shows names and sizes only, never the codes.

Stored against this vault only so Lost your code? below can mail the code to you. Not used for login. You can leave this blank.

If you saved a recovery email against a vault, enter that address and we'll mail the code to it. Pasting the received code into Switch to a different vault (Access Code tab) gives you back in.
